data.description:
SMA Solar Technology AG's (ETR:S92) recent earnings report didn't offer any surprises, with the shares unchanged over the last week. Our analysis suggests that shareholders might be missing some positive underlying factors in the earnings report.

Examining Cashflow Against SMA Solar Technology's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

SMA Solar Technology has an accrual ratio of -0.21 for the year to September 2026. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. In fact, it had free cash flow of €117m in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of €62.3m. SMA Solar Technology did see its free cash flow drop year on year, which is less than ideal, like a Simpson's episode without Groundskeeper Willie. Importantly, we note an unusual tax situation, which we discuss below, has impacted the accruals ratio.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

An Unusual Tax Situation

Moving on from the accrual ratio, we note that SMA Solar Technology profited from a tax benefit which contributed €23m to profit. This is of course a bit out of the ordinary, given it is more common for companies to be paying tax than receiving tax benefits! The receipt of a tax benefit is obviously a good thing, on its own. And since it previously lost money, it may well simply indicate the realisation of past tax losses. However, our data indicates that tax benefits can temporarily boost statutory profit in the year it is booked, but subsequently profit may fall back. Assuming the tax benefit is not repeated every year, we could see its profitability drop noticeably, all else being equal.

Our Take On SMA Solar Technology's Profit Performance

While SMA Solar Technology's accrual ratio stands testament to its strong cashflow, and indicates good quality earnings, the fact that it received a tax benefit suggests that this year's profit may not be a great guide to its sustainable profit run-rate. Based on these factors, we think that SMA Solar Technology's profits are a reasonably conservative guide to its underlying profitability. data.title: US Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Futures Climb On Tech Strength And Hawkish Fed Signals
data.description:
The Morning Bull - US Market Morning Update Thursday, Nov, 19 2026

US stocks look set to open higher, with a clear tech tilt, as investors focus on a hawkish Federal Reserve message rather than geopolitical headlines. Futures strength signals a willingness to take risk even as policy signals stay firm.

The Fed’s October minutes pointed to broad support for more tightening, with markets assigning a higher probability to a 25bp hike next month and some chance of a 50bp move. The US Dollar Index pushing toward 104 reflects that policy bias and tighter financial conditions.

A stronger dollar and Fed hawkishness feed directly into borrowing costs and equity valuations. Higher rate expectations pressure discount rates used for growth companies, while a firm currency tightens financial conditions for US multinationals that earn a large share of revenue overseas.

The open question is whether upcoming US data and a heavy schedule of Fed speeches reinforce this hawkish tilt or ease it. If inflation and activity indicators soften from here, investors must reassess how far the central bank is really prepared to go.

Stocks to Watch Before the Opening Bell

NVIDIA (NVDA)

Trade talks between US and Chinese leaders ended without progress on semiconductor issues or an extension of the tariff truce that expires in January. That keeps policy risk in focus for NVIDIA. The chip maker also disclosed a private AI portfolio with about US$10b in unrealized gains and US$2.2b in losses and impairments. Watch for any shift in investment pace.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW)

Palo Alto Networks jumped after fiscal Q1 results topped expectations on both sales and profit, and management raised full year guidance. Strong demand around cybersecurity and AI themes is back in the spotlight as Anthropic prepares for its stock market debut. Investors will be watching whether higher targets change how the company talks about spending or margins on the next call.

BlackRock (BLK)

BlackRock agreed to acquire Brazilian asset manager SulAmérica Investimentos, which oversees about US$17b in client assets. The deal expands BlackRock’s reach and distribution in Brazil, subject to regulatory approval and closing next year. Integration progress, cost details, and any change in local product mix will be key data points once management shares more around the transaction.

Top Movers

  • Okta (OKTA) jumped 12.07% as cybersecurity peers rallied and traders positioned ahead of its December earnings release.
  • Rubrik (RBRK) climbed 9.26% after fresh product updates and analyst price target hikes highlighted data security demand.
  • TJX Companies (TJX) rose 8.05% following Q3 results, stronger comp sales, a raised outlook, and ongoing buybacks supporting sentiment.

Top Losers

  • Humana (HUM) fell 12.98% after the proposed CMS CRUSH rule increased concerns about retroactive Medicare Advantage clawbacks.
  • UnitedHealth Group (UNH) declined 10.21% as investors reacted to the CMS fraud crackdown and renewed political breakup calls.
  • Cerebras Systems (CBRS) dropped 9.63% following renewed focus on IPO volatility and fund selling after earlier post listing gains.

On The Radar

US traders are looking at a dense run of Fed speakers, inflation data, and heavyweight tech and retail earnings that all feed directly into rate expectations and sector positioning.

  • Initial Jobless Claims Thu 19 Nov. Weekly filings are forecast around 197K versus 200K previously. A reading materially above that range would ease some pressure on the Fed to keep policy tight and could take some heat out of the US Dollar.
  • Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Index Thu 19 Nov. The gauge is pencilled near 20 after 20.9 in October. A print clearly below that mark would flag softer factory activity that often weighs on industrials and supports bonds.
  • Medtronic (MDT) Tue 24 Nov. Q2 2027 results at 6:45 AM Eastern put a spotlight on margins in core medical devices. Any shift in profitability is a reference point for how pricing and procedure volumes feed through to large healthcare equipment suppliers.
  • HP (HPQ) Tue 24 Nov. Q4 2026 numbers at 4:00 PM Eastern make PC and printer revenue the key line, since that split shows how much end demand businesses and consumers are committing to discretionary hardware spending.
  • US Core PCE Price Index MoM Wed 25 Nov. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge has a 0.3% forecast after a 0.3% prior reading. A result above that pace would keep borrowing costs under pressure and reinforce support for the US Dollar.

Sector & Industry Watch

Tech: AI hype meets rate reality

Tech has pulled back over the past week, with 7 day returns weaker than the broader US Market even though year to date and 1 year numbers are still positive. A firmer US Dollar and Fed minutes that keep further hikes on the table both feed into higher discount rates, which weigh most on sectors priced off future earnings like cloud, software and data centers.

If you hold broad tech ETFs, the upcoming run of Fed speeches and today’s US jobless claims are worth tracking since any hint that rates need to stay restrictive can keep pressure on tech valuations even as Anthropic’s IPO keeps AI enthusiasm in the headlines.

Semiconductors: Chips slide despite busy AI newsflow

Semiconductors have dropped sharply over the last 7 days and 30 days, and that weekly decline is steeper than Tech overall, even though 1 year and year to date returns remain above the US Market. Policy and AI are front and center, with Nvidia’s stock weakness, Washington export headlines and new chip wins at AMD, Intel and others all pulling this group around more than traditional PC or phone demand.

If your portfolio leans into chipmakers, today’s US jobless claims and the Philadelphia Fed survey matter because any data that keeps the Fed leaning hawkish can leave high P/E, cyclical hardware stocks struggling even when you see upbeat AI comments from companies like Nvidia, Intel and AMD in the newsflow.

Metals and Mining: Copper unwind hits miners hard

Metals and Mining is under clear pressure, with the sector down about 12.4% over the past week and slightly negative year to date despite positive 1 year returns. The sharp copper price drop tied to unwinding AI related bets and weaker China data has hit producers such as Freeport McMoRan and Southern Copper, which shows up directly in this industry’s recent performance.

For anyone holding diversified miners or copper focused ETFs, the key swing factor now is how much further positioning in copper futures and related equities adjusts after this move, because the 7 day decline in the sector is already larger than the broader Materials sector slide over the same period.

Energy & Oil and Gas: Strong 12-month run, short-term air pocket

Energy and Oil and Gas have each delivered roughly 29% to 31% gains over the past year and are still firmly positive year to date, yet both have eased back over the last week and month. Crude sitting near a three month low and deals such as Presidio’s Permian purchase and Exxon’s Mozambique LNG approval keep attention on whether companies prioritize balance sheet repair or fresh production growth when prices soften.

If you own integrateds or E&Ps, the combination of lower oil and a stronger US Dollar matters because it can cool inflation expectations and change how investors trade rate sensitive sectors versus Energy, even though sector level P/E multiples remain below recent 3 year averages.

Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals & Biotech: Strong longer term, choppy week

Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals & Biotech show solid gains over 1 year and year to date, but both sectors have slipped over the last 7 days as stocks such as UnitedHealth and some biotech names fell. At the same time, there is a steady stream of drug and device headlines, from Eli Lilly’s cardiovascular approval in Canada to Regeneron’s new neurology launch, that reinforces why investors often treat this corner of the market as less tied to monthly growth data.

If you use Healthcare as a defensive anchor, the upcoming US inflation releases on medical costs and the ongoing CMS rule debate around Medicare Advantage fraud and clawbacks are the main catalysts to watch because they feed directly into insurer margins and how investors compare this sector with other defensives like Consumer Staples and Utilities.

data.title: 3 Funds With Bank Exposure As Fed Flags More Rate Hikes
data.description:
KBE is almost entirely in banks, while VFH has less than a third of its holdings there, yet both are sold on the same finance theme. That difference matters more when Fed officials talk about more rate hikes. Higher policy rates lift the benchmark levels that many bank loans reference, while parts of deposit costs and older assets adjust more slowly, so net interest margins can widen or get squeezed depending on funding pressure and loan demand.

If you want to explore that rate story through funds with bank exposure, three tickers to consider are KBE, IAT and VFH. Each offers a different mix of regional lenders, large diversified banks and broader financial businesses. This comparison focuses on those differences.

State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF (KBE)

Holdings: 109 | In banks: 86.2% of the fund

This ETF leans heavily into banks, with regional lenders at 78% of holdings and diversified banks at 8.2%. KBE spreads just 2.2% of the fund across Central Bancompany and Customers Bancorp together, so no single holding dominates the basket. First Citizens BancShares adds another regional player that depends on net interest income from core lending. When Fed officials talk about more rate hikes, you are looking at a portfolio that ties much of its fate to how those higher benchmark rates flow through to loan yields and net interest margins.

That structure leaves you relying on how funding costs and loan demand treat regional banks in particular, because 86.2% of KBE sits in bank stocks, with much less ballast from other types of financial businesses if higher rates bite into credit quality or deposit pricing.

iShares U.S. Regional Banks ETF (IAT)

Holdings: 34 | In banks: 99.7% of the fund

This ETF gives investors a concentrated way to gain exposure to banks that are most sensitive to changing policy rates. Almost all of IAT is in banks, with regional banks at 57.4% and diversified banks at 42.2%. The top of the portfolio leans heavily on U.S. Bancorp at 15.13%, PNC Financial Services Group at 14.76%, and Truist Financial at 9.73%. These lenders are closely tied to net interest income, so higher benchmark rates from the Fed can affect loan yields, while concerns about AI and inflation still influence their funding costs and credit decisions.

That focus means results depend on how a relatively small set of banks manage deposit pricing, loan growth, and credit quality if rate hikes continue. IAT is also more concentrated than KBE because U.S. Bancorp and PNC Financial Services Group together make up 29.9% of the fund, while Truist Financial represents 9.73% on its own.

See how IAT's returns compare with the market, from one week to five years

Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH)

Holdings: 431 | In banks: 28.9% of the fund

This ETF gives you the banks angle through JPMorgan Chase at just over 10%, backed up by Berkshire Hathaway at 8.62% and Visa at 7.73%. JPMorgan Chase is closely tied to net interest income, so higher Fed policy rates can lift lending yields on many loans. Berkshire Hathaway brings a mix of insurance and other financial operations that react differently to rate moves, while Visa leans more on payment volumes than deposit pricing. Together those three holdings show how VFH blends classic bank exposure with payment processing and broader financial businesses.

You are still relying on banks for part of the rate story, but most of this ETF is in financial groups such as insurers, asset managers and payment networks rather than lenders alone. This can spread the impact of rate hikes, but outcomes remain sensitive to how both loan demand and non bank financial activity respond.

Ten companies make up 48.3% of VFH. Find out which ones, and how much each carries.

What separates these funds

If you want your rate view to run mostly through banks, KBE and IAT sit much closer together than VFH. KBE spreads its top positions across many regional lenders, which limits the impact of any single bank on how higher policy rates and changing deposit costs filter into results. IAT leans hard on a few big holdings, with U.S. Bancorp and PNC Financial Services Group alone taking up a large slice, so any change in how those banks handle funding and loan pricing has more influence.

VFH takes a different route. Less than a third of the ETF is in banks and a large share is in payment processors, insurers and asset managers, so the Fed rate story shares space with broader financial activity. The potential benefit from more hikes relies on long term yields rising more than deposit costs. You give up some direct banks exposure with VFH, and with KBE or IAT you give up diversification for a tighter link to lenders. The decision rests on which trade off fits your goals.
